hook_clip: Here's how to reverse engineer Chaser from a written spec. Claude passed all eighteen checks, but my spec never said if an import could undo a payment.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: We gave Claude one Markdown file. It copies the part of Chaser a small team actually uses. Open invoices imported from your accounting software's CSV export. A reminder schedule, from a heads-up before the due date to a final notice. One email per customer per day. And an aging report.

The core rule is simple. Never chase what shouldn't be chased. Paid, disputed and written-off invoices are never included. Neither are paused customers, or an invoice with a promise to pay that hasn't passed. So on the seed day, Kestrel Schools is skipped, because they promised to pay by October twentieth. And Harbor Clinic is skipped, because it's paused.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. Invoices and import. The schedule, templates and the daily run. Payments, promises, disputes and calls. Then reports and export. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser, from fresh seed data.

Here's what it built. The invoices list shows seven open invoices, thirty-one thousand eight hundred dollars, with twenty thousand five hundred overdue. Today's run sends Acme Corp one email that lists both their invoices, seven thousand three hundred dollars in all. With sending switched off, that email waits in the outbox. When Kestrel's promise date passes unpaid, the promise is marked broken, and reminders resume. And the aging report splits every balance by how late it is.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all eighteen checks passed, along with one hundred and thirteen automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The test build exposed eighty-three places where Claude had to guess. Customers created by an import had no account owner, so the promise-broken email had nobody to go to. With sending off, a held final notice never reached the customer, and nothing said if it started the seven days before a phone call. And a due date moved later on import could send a gentler reminder after a firmer one. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't the same as production-ready. We didn't test production sign-in, real email delivery, a hosted scheduler, or real accounting exports. The reminder job was triggered by hand, on a development clock.

So is it worth building? Chaser prices its plans by your company's revenue. In the United States, Compact is two hundred and thirty-three dollars a month billed yearly, for up to four users. Core is seven hundred, and Complete one thousand and fifty. That's two thousand seven hundred and ninety-six dollars a year at the bottom. If you want live accounting sync, a payment portal or SMS, buy it. If you chase late invoices from a spreadsheet, and your accounting software exports a CSV, build it.
Everything is in one file. The data model, ten rules, seed data, four phase prompts, and all eighteen checks, with the eighty-three fixes already in.
